To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prenatal glucocorticoid exposure programs adult hypertension in the offspring.
the fetal environment is critical for programming of the cardiovascular system and that the mechanisms involved in the programming process involve glucocorticoids and epigenetic modifications.

1) the fetal environment can program adult hypertension, 2) this programming occurs via the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis, and 3) the mechanisms of programming are likely to involve glucocorticoid action.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying the programming of adult hypertension by glucocorticoids and by poor nutrition in the fetal and neonatal periods.
understanding the mechanisms underlying the association between poor intra‐uterile growth and the Metabolic and Cardiovascular diseases.
the effects of glucocorticoids and other stressors on fetal growth and development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prenatal undernutrition is a major determinant of adult hypertension, and the glucocorticoid hypothesis is the major underlying mechanism for this effect.
prenatal undernutrition, in the absence of postnatal undernutrition, does not program the development of hypertension in adult life.
prenatal undernutrition is associated with increased risk of adult hypertension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fetal brain is a major organ of glucocorticoid action and that glucocorticoids are a major factor in the programming of adult hypertension and the Metabolic Syndrome.
the effects of glucocorticoids are mediated by the glucocorticoid receptor (GR), and that GR expression and function is modulated by the epigenetic state of the promoter region.
prenatal undernutrition, glucocorticoids, and the programming of hypertension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should be more careful when prescribing glucocorticoids to pregnant women.
prenatal stress and glucocorticoid exposure may be an important mechanism by which early life events influence adult disease.
